title: A Practical Benchmark of Image-Restoration Networks for ASL Perfusion-Weighted Image Denoising
authors: Shaokang Wen, He Wang, Zhensen Chen, Hongwei Li
synopsis: Low signal-to-noise ratio limits the quality of ASL perfusion-weighted images, and the choice of denoising architecture remains task-dependent.
To compare established image-restoration networks and inform model selection for ASL PWI denoising.
Four networks were evaluated with pseudo-3D and volumetric inputs and with direct and residual prediction, using 217 training and 54 validation cases. Two classical methods served as comparators.

The 3D residual transformer models performed similarly. Swin U-Net achieved the highest mean SSIM and PSNR and the lowest RMSE; SwinIR achieved the lowest NMSE. Residual prediction substantially improved U-Net.
impact: This comparison informs the selection of image-restoration models for ASL PWI denoising and characterizes the influence of input dimensionality and output formulation on performance.
introduction: Arterial spin labeling (ASL) enables noninvasive perfusion imaging but is limited by low signal-to-noise ratio. Mean control–label difference images, termed perfusion-weighted images (PWI), provide useful information for visual assessment of perfusion abnormalities [1]. Building on previous ASL denoising studies [2,3], we compared established image-restoration architectures within a common PWI processing and evaluation framework to guide model selection for this application.
methods: The dataset comprised 271 cases: 67 healthy controls, 103 stroke cases, 59 obstructive sleep apnea cases, 14 ______ cases, and 28 ______ cases. There were 217 training and 54 validation cases. All acquisitions used a GRASE readout. PLDs were 1500 ms (79 cases), 1800 ms (124 cases), and 2000 ms (68 cases). Cases with substantial head motion were excluded, and included data underwent motion correction. Volumes had a 64 × 64 matrix, 22–28 slices, and approximately 3.5 × 3.5 × 6 mm voxels. Inputs averaged four PWI repetitions; references averaged 18 repetitions, including the four used in the input. Both network inputs and targets were PWI.

U-Net [4], Pix2Pix [5], SwinIR [2,6], and a Swin U-Net based on the HUST framework [3] were adapted to three-slice pseudo-3D and volumetric 3D inputs. Task-specific modifications included single-channel PWI regression, adjusted feature widths and attention windows, and anisotropic operations in volumetric models. Direct image prediction and residual prediction, in which the network output is added to the input, were evaluated for each network, yielding 16 configurations. Three-slice input was informed by Shou et al.’s reported balance between noise reduction and CBF bias [2]. Their observation of increased white matter CBF bias with M0-assisted denoising motivated the exclusion of M0 as an input channel. M0 was used only to define a foreground mask. Classical comparators were BM4D and DT-CWT-NLM [7,8].

Input images and references shared min–max scaling derived from the input, without clipping. Training used 48 × 48 pseudo-3D crops or 16 × 48 × 48 volumetric crops, paired in-plane augmentation, Adam with an initial learning rate of 0.0002, and at most 200 epochs. All networks used a foreground-masked loss combining equally weighted L1 and SSIM terms. Pix2Pix additionally used a foreground-weighted adversarial loss with weight 0.01 and coordinated learning-rate decay for the generator and discriminator. Checkpoints were selected by mean validation reconstruction loss. All methods were evaluated within the same M0-derived foreground mask on 54 validation cases. SSIM and PSNR used the common intensity scale defined by the input PWI range. MAE and RMSE used original PWI intensities, whereas NMSE normalized squared error by reference signal energy. Metrics were calculated per case and summarized as the mean and sample standard deviation, with equal weighting of cases.
results: Input PWI had a mean SSIM of 0.8618, PSNR of 33.40 dB, RMSE of 8.87, and NMSE of 0.3148. BM4D and DT-CWT-NLM reduced RMSE to 8.41 and 8.18, respectively. SwinIR and Swin U-Net achieved PSNR values of 37.19–37.43 dB across the evaluated configurations. The 3D residual Swin U-Net achieved the highest mean SSIM (0.9220) and PSNR (37.43 dB), and the lowest RMSE (5.44). The corresponding SwinIR achieved the lowest NMSE (0.1052), compared with 0.1055 for Swin U-Net. Their performance was closely matched, with differences of only 0.0003 in SSIM, 0.03 dB in PSNR, and 0.02 in RMSE.

Residual prediction improved U-Net PSNR from 24.94 to 36.87 dB in pseudo-3D and from 29.94 to 36.86 dB in 3D. Pix2Pix achieved 35.70–35.94 dB. Volumetric transformer models improved PSNR by 0.05–0.23 dB over the corresponding pseudo-3D models. Table 1 summarizes all configurations, Figures 1 and 2 show the distributions across cases, and Figure 3 presents representative PWI comparisons.
discussion: SwinIR and Swin U-Net provided the strongest aggregate performance, with small differences between them under the evaluated conditions. Three-slice pseudo-3D models achieved results close to those of volumetric transformers, and residual U-Net provided a competitive convolutional alternative. These findings indicate that output formulation warrants consideration alongside network architecture. All networks shared the same PWI denoising task and reconstruction loss. Model sizes differed, and Pix2Pix additionally incorporated an adversarial loss. The validation set also guided checkpoint selection, only one random seed was evaluated, and the input and reference shared noise. These factors limit conclusions about generalization and stable differences between architectures.
